### 1.1 Before listening (2 minutes, Arabic is fine here)

1. Where do you keep the work you are doing now?
2. What do you do when the electricity stops in the middle of your work?
3. How many copies of your most important file do you have?

### 1.4 Now read the passage

### Passage: *The Night the Network Failed* (320 words)

Last March, Omar was finishing his final project at the computer centre. He was studying software engineering, and the project was the most important work of his year. The college wanted it on Friday morning.

**[A]** On Tuesday evening, he was sitting at his usual desk. The room was quiet. Three other students were working near the window, and the lights were low. Omar was uploading his files to the college server when the screen stopped moving.

At first he was not worried. The internet in the building was often slow, so he waited. He checked the cable. He restarted the browser. Nothing changed on the screen. The upload was stuck at sixty per cent.

**[B]** Then the lights went out. The electricity was off, and the room was completely dark. The other students were laughing, because this happened almost every week. Omar was not laughing. His computer turned off while it was writing to the server, and he did not know which files arrived and which did not.

When the power came back, twenty minutes later, he opened his folder again. The file was there, but it was broken. The computer could not open it. He tried it again, and then he tried it on another machine. Three months of work were inside that file.

**[C]** Then he remembered something his teacher said in the first week: "Save often, and save in two places." He opened his email. While he was uploading the file that evening, he also sent a copy to himself — not because he was careful, but because he wanted to read it at home.

The copy was from Sunday. It was two days old.

**[D]** Omar finished the project that night. He slept for four hours. In the morning, before his class, he bought a small USB drive. Now, when he is working on something important, he saves it in three places: the computer, his email, and the drive.

### 1.5 Read aloud

Read the passage aloud **once** and record it. Compare it with your Lesson 2 recording: are you stopping less often?

parts.title: Grammar — the past continuous
parts.markdown:
We use the past continuous for an action that was **in the middle of happening** in the past: *At eight o'clock, Omar **was uploading** his files.*

### 3.1 How we make it

**was / were** + verb **-ing**

| Person | Past continuous |
|---|---|
| I / he / she / it | **was** working |
| you / we / they | **were** working |

### 3.2 What we use it for

- An action in the middle of happening: *At eight o'clock he **was uploading** his files.*
- A long action stopped by a short one: *He **was uploading** his files **when** the screen stopped.*
- Two long actions at the same time: ***While** the students **were laughing**, Omar **was looking** at his screen.*
- The background of a story: *The room was quiet. Three students **were working** near the window.*

### 3.4 Past simple or past continuous?

| Past simple — the short, finished action | Past continuous — the longer action around it |
|---|---|
| The screen **stopped**. | He **was uploading** his files. |
| The lights **went** out. | The students **were working**. |
| The computer **turned** off. | It **was writing** to the server. |

The rule to remember: **when** + past simple, **while** + past continuous.

### 3.5 Negative and question

|  | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Negative | **was not / were not** + *-ing* | Omar **was not laughing**. |
| Question | **Was / Were** + person + *-ing* | **Were** the students **laughing**? |

### 3.6 Grammar practice

**A. Put the verb in the past continuous:**

1. At eight o'clock, Omar \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (sit) at his usual desk.
2. Three students \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (work) near the window.
3. The computer turned off while it \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (write) to the server.
4. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ the students \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (laugh)?
5. Omar \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not laugh).

**B. Choose the past simple or the past continuous:**

1. He (uploaded / was uploading) his files when the screen (stopped / was stopping).
2. While the power (was / was being) off, the students (talked / were talking).
3. He (found / was finding) the email while he (looked / was looking) for the file.

parts.title: The sounds of was and were
parts.markdown: ### 3.3 The two sounds of *was* and *were* (listen to `05-weak-forms.mp3`) In a sentence, *was* and *were* are almost always **weak** — short and quiet. They are **strong** only at the end of a sentence, or when we want to insist that something is true. | Word | Weak (normal, inside a sentence) | Strong (at the end, or to insist) | |---|---|---| | was | /wəz/ | /wɒz/ | | were | /wə/ | /wɜː/ | | Weak | Strong | |---|---| | *He was working at his desk.* | *Yes, he was.* | | *The room was quiet.* | *It was.* | | *Three students were working near the window.* | *Yes, they were.* | | *The lights were low.* | *They were.* | In the audio you hear each pair twice, then a short test: say whether the *was* or *were* you hear is **weak** or **strong**, then listen to the answer.

segments.say: Pronunciation. The two sounds of was and were.
Inside a sentence, was and were are weak: short and quiet. At the end of a sentence, or when we insist that something is true, they are strong. Listen to each pair, then repeat.
He was working at his desk.
Three students were working near the window.
Now the test. You will hear a sentence. Say whether the was or the were you hear is weak or strong. Then you will hear the answer.
This is the end of the pronunciation practice.

parts.title: Writing — The Day Something Stopped My Work
parts.markdown:
### 5.2 Writing — "The Day Something Stopped My Work" (10–12 sentences)

**Model answer (copy the shape, change the words):**

> Last year, I was writing a long report for my course. I was working at home in the evening, and the room was quiet. While I was typing, the electricity stopped. My laptop had no battery, so the screen went dark. At first I was angry, because I did not save the file. I waited for two hours. When the power came back, I opened the file again. The computer showed an old version from the morning. I lost three hours of work. Now I save my work every ten minutes, and I keep a copy on a USB drive. It is a small habit, but it helps.

**Checklist before you send it:**

- [ ] I used the past continuous for the long action (*I was writing*, *while I was typing*).
- [ ] I used the past simple for the short action that stopped it (*the electricity stopped*).
- [ ] I used **when** with the past simple and **while** with the past continuous.
- [ ] I used at least **5 new words** from Session 2.
- [ ] I used at least **2 words** from Lesson 1 or Lesson 2.
- [ ] Capital letters and full stops are correct.
- [ ] My text has 10–12 sentences.

parts.title: Answer key and teacher notes
parts.markdown:
**Listening:** L1 — Omar, software engineering · L2 — uploading his files to the college server · L3 — a copy he had sent to his own email · L4 — two days old (from Sunday)

**Part A (MCQ):** 1-B · 2-B · 3-C · 4-A · 5-C · 6-C · 7-D · 8-B

*Why 7 is **[D]***: the sentence says the copy opened, so it can only follow *"The copy was from Sunday. It was two days old."* At **[C]** it would contradict the broken file described just before it.

*Why 8 is **[B]***: the teacher's words are what make Omar think of his email, so that paragraph exists to explain how he found the second copy — not to describe Omar, and not to blame the college.

**Part B (True/False):**

1. F — He was studying software engineering.
2. T
3. F — Omar was not laughing.
4. T
5. F — It was from Sunday.
6. T

**Part C (Fill in the blanks):** 1. project · 2. server · 3. stuck, per cent · 4. cable, browser · 5. broken · 6. Save
*(Extra words: version, careful)*

**2.4 A (Opposites):** 1. download · 2. careless · 3. working / fine · 4. quiet / silent · 5. start / begin

**2.4 B (Odd one out):** 1. evening (the others are computer words) · 2. project (the others are things you can touch) · 3. careful (the others mean damaged or not moving)

**3.6 A (Past continuous):** 1. was sitting · 2. were working · 3. was writing · 4. Were … laughing · 5. was not laughing
**3.6 B (Simple or continuous):** 1. was uploading, stopped · 2. was, were talking · 3. found, was looking

**Mini-quiz:** 1. was working · 2. were laughing · 3. when, while · 4. download · 5. careless · 6. server · 7. browser · 8. stuck · 9–12. teacher judgement

### Teacher Notes {: #teacher-notes }

**What changed from Lesson 2.** The passage grew from 244 to 320 words, the past continuous joins the past simple, and an eighth question type — purpose of a paragraph — joins sentence insertion. The pronunciation slot moves from the three sounds of *-ed* to the weak forms of *was* and *were*. The order of the sessions, the self-report and the six original TOEFL question types are deliberately unchanged, so only one thing is new at a time.

**The one real difficulty.** Not the form — *was* + *-ing* is easy to build — but knowing when to choose it. Arabic marks the progressive past differently, so the student will reach for the past simple everywhere and say *while I worked, the power stopped*. Drill the pair in 3.4 until *while* automatically pulls *-ing* behind it.

**Why this story.** The vocabulary is the vocabulary of her actual working life: server, upload, browser, version, save. She is about to carry application files, scans and transcripts between machines, and the passage teaches that problem while teaching the tense. It is also the third story in a row in which the lesson is *keep a second copy* — that repetition is intentional.

**Success criteria for Lesson 3.** The student should be able to:

- answer L1–L4 correctly on the second hearing;
- retell the story in 5–6 sentences using at least two past-continuous verbs;
- choose correctly between past simple and past continuous in 3.6 B;
- hear the difference between weak and strong *was*;
- use 10 of the 14 key words in her own sentence;
- write 10 sentences about a personal past event with fewer than 4 tense errors.

**If it is too easy:** Lesson 4 goes to 400 words, adds the present perfect (*I have saved it*), and the MCQ set adds a rhetorical-purpose question about the whole passage.
**If it is too hard:** keep the same passage for a second week, drop question 8, and drill only 3.1 and 3.4.

**A note on spaced recall.** `03-vocabulary.mp3` ends with five Lesson 1 words — *check, centre, tool, slow, wake up* — which are the five she has **not** heard since Lesson 1, because Lesson 2 recalled the other five. Lesson 2's own words come back in Lesson 4. Keep that two-lesson gap: it is the gap, not the repetition, that moves a word into long-term memory.

segments.say: Slow version. The passage, read slowly, one time.

Last March, Omar was finishing his final project at the computer centre. He was studying software engineering, and the project was the most important work of his year. The college wanted it on Friday morning.

On Tuesday evening, he was sitting at his usual desk. The room was quiet. Three other students were working near the window, and the lights were low. Omar was uploading his files to the college server when the screen stopped moving.

At first he was not worried. The internet in the building was often slow, so he waited. He checked the cable. He restarted the browser. Nothing changed on the screen. The upload was stuck at sixty per cent.

Then the lights went out. The electricity was off, and the room was completely dark. The other students were laughing, because this happened almost every week. Omar was not laughing. His computer turned off while it was writing to the server, and he did not know which files arrived and which did not.

When the power came back, twenty minutes later, he opened his folder again. The file was there, but it was broken. The computer could not open it. He tried it again, and then he tried it on another machine. Three months of work were inside that file.

Then he remembered something his teacher said in the first week: "Save often, and save in two places." He opened his email. While he was uploading the file that evening, he also sent a copy to himself — not because he was careful, but because he wanted to read it at home.

The copy was from Sunday. It was two days old.

Omar finished the project that night. He slept for four hours. In the morning, before his class, he bought a small USB drive. Now, when he is working on something important, he saves it in three places: the computer, his email, and the drive.
